source.title: An Effective and Efficient Initialization Scheme for Multi-layer Feedforward Neural Networks
source.authors: Zebin Yang; Hengtao Zhang; A. Sudjianto; Aijun Zhang

record.tranche_reason: The paper compares initialization methods and reports their effect on training-loss trajectories, using a supervised Stein-based initialization rather than the random initialization methods described in V4.
record.gate_note: The paper tests initialization effects on training loss and speed. It does not report CIFAR results or training classification error; test RMSE and AUC results are not training-error results. Results cited from other papers are not recorded as this study’s findings.
record.test_reason: The reported results compare the authors' supervised SteinGLM initialization with benchmark initializations. They do not establish V4's activation-matched signal/gradient preservation effect or its orthogonal-versus-Gaussian comparison at equal variance. The method incorporates orthogonal weights, but reporting its superior performance alone does not test those claims.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the authors' conclusion: SteinGLM improves training convergence and reported predictive performance in their feedforward experiments. In the MNIST CNN demonstration, training is faster but validation and test performance show no significant difference. The supplied training curves are indexed by epochs, so they do not independently establish total wall-clock savings including supervised initialization.
record.recipe_differences: The paper proposes supervised Stein identity and GLM initialization and compares it with Glorot Normal, He Normal, and Orthogonal initialization; its method is not the random initialization intervention described in V4.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported training-loss results cover regression versus binary classification tasks and feedforward networks versus the CNN demonstration. The reported CNN training-speed improvement is accompanied by no significant validation or test performance difference.

fits_no_version.finding: Supervised SteinGLM initialization produces faster training-loss convergence than Glorot Normal, He Normal, and Orthogonal in the reported feedforward and MNIST CNN experiments.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Response-informed Stein/GLM initialization can accelerate training relative to standard initialization methods in these tested settings.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors collectively describe the three benchmark initializations as susceptible to less optimal training solutions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Standard initialization benchmarks can converge to worse training solutions than SteinGLM in these experiments; the supplied text does not separate this finding by benchmark.

record.problems: Training-loss trajectories are shown in figures and summarized qualitatively in text; exact loss values and training-trajectory uncertainty are not stated. The stated benchmark difficulty is grouped across three methods rather than reported separately for each. The experiments use UCI datasets and a small MNIST CNN demonstration, not the benchmark settings named in most claim versions.
record.rows_left_out: Test RMSE and AUC values in Tables 2–5 are generalization measures, not training classification error or training-loss outcomes for the claim. No other qualifying training results were omitted.

untested.parts: Near-zero training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, including random or corrupted labels and model-size or training-recipe qualifications.
Spurious local minima and extra student neurons in two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems.
Training degradation with depth, identity shortcuts, and the specified plain-network or Fixup exceptions.

Activation-matched initialization preserving signals and gradients; resulting speed and trainable-depth benefits; orthogonal versus Gaussian weights of equal variance; and 10,000-layer plain CNN training.
Stability thresholds, loss recovery, curvature dynamics, and divergence.
Batch normalization's training-speed and learning-rate benefits, and the Fixup comparison.

record.verdict_notes: The benchmark difficulty statement does not justify limits_scope for V4: outperforming an initialization does not show that its claimed benefit is absent or incomplete. The supplied text contains figure captions but no readable curve values establishing a separate orthogonal-versus-Gaussian comparison.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 training classification error, random or corrupted labels, and effects of model size or training duration on near-zero error are not tested.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems, spurious minima, and teacher/student width are not tested.
Plain versus residual networks and the effects of depth or shortcuts on training error are not tested.

The study tests training speed across network depths with tanh activations, but not whether matched initializations prevent signal or gradient vanishing/explosion, orthogonal versus Gaussian weights of equal variance in the specified tanh setting, or 10,000-layer plain CNNs.
Learning rates above stability limits, curvature, and loss recovery or divergence are not tested.
Batch normalization and its effect on speed or learning-rate tolerance are not tested.

rows.subject: SteinGLM
rows.size_stated: 10, 20, 30, and 40 hidden layers; min{d, 20} neurons per layer
rows.operation_detail: Train networks initialized with SteinGLM and compare training-loss trajectories.

conditions.value: five real-world datasets; averaged across datasets and ten repetitions
Adam, initial learning rate 0.001; maximal 200 epochs

rows.measure: Averaged training-loss trajectories; authors report convergence much faster than benchmarks.
rows.baseline: Glorot Normal, He Normal, and Orthogonal initialization
rows.value: Networks initialized with SteinGLM converge much faster than the benchmarks.
rows.note: Figure curves are averaged over the tested datasets and ten repetitions; exact training-loss values are not stated in the text.
rows.check: SteinGLM's faster regression training is the proposed method's performance, not a test of V4's specified initialization effects.

rows.operation_detail: Initialize CNN layers with SteinGLM and compare training-loss curves with other initialization methods.

conditions.value: binary classification on MNIST digit pairs (3, 5), (4, 9), (7, 9), and (5, 8)

rows.measure: Training-loss curves; authors report SteinGLM converges much faster in each binary classification task.
rows.baseline: Glorot Normal, He Normal, and Orthogonal initialization
rows.value: The proposed SteinGLM algorithm converges much faster in each binary classification task.
rows.note: Authors report no significant difference among methods in validation and test performance; this row records training loss only.
rows.check: The MNIST experiment reports the proposed supervised initialization's training advantage at one CNN depth, without testing activation matching, signal preservation, or the specified orthogonal-kernel depth result.
